# Whitespace

Source: *The UI/UX Playbook* (uxpeak). Each entry separates **what the PDF states** from **our interpretation of its images**. Text explanations are complete without the images. Back to the [index](../index.md).

| ID | Principle | PDF pages |
|---|---|---|
| [WS-01](#ws-01) | Give elements room to breathe | 25, 26 |
| [WS-02](#ws-02) | Start with too much space, then scale down | 26, 27 |

<a id="ws-01"></a>
## WS-01 - Give elements room to breathe

Whitespace (any empty area, whatever its colour) improves readability, guides focus and breaks up the page; too little feels cramped.

- **Source:** PDF 25 (printed 24), 26 (printed 25)
- **Applies when:** Navigation, cards, lists, any dense surface.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Whitespace is the unmarked area between elements; it can be any colour, texture or background as long as it is free of other elements.
- Lack of whitespace makes designs cramped, confusing and overwhelming; even when fonts, positions and colours are the same, spacing can make or break the design.

**Mistake:** Tight padding around a logo, cramped dividers and groups packed together (e.g. sidebar).  
**Effect:** Hard to scan; feels overwhelming.

**Correction:** Add vertical space around the logo and between items and groups; accept fewer items per view.  
**Why it works:** Space separates groups and lets users find items without overload.

**Observable checks:**
- Is spacing between groups clearly larger than spacing within a group?
- Do any texts touch or nearly touch container edges or dividers?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- WS-02: too much space is also wrong as a final state; balance is the goal.

**Related:** [WS-02](08-whitespace.md#ws-02), [WS-03](08-whitespace.md#ws-03), [PRX-01](03-proximity.md#prx-01)

<a id="ws-02"></a>
## WS-02 - Start with too much space, then scale down

Begin with more space than you think you need and reduce gradually to the right balance; starting tight hides clutter.

- **Source:** PDF 26 (printed 25), 27 (printed 26)
- **Applies when:** Laying out a new component or screen.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Too much space is a better starting point than too little.
- Start generous and scale down gradually; if you start with too little you may not notice the clutter.
- Both an over-spaced and a cramped version of the same card are shown as incorrect; the balanced version is correct.

**Mistake:** Final designs that are either cramped or excessively spaced.  
**Effect:** Cramped: hard to look at and navigate. Over-spaced: content feels disconnected.

**Correction:** Iterate from generous to balanced, keeping consistent gaps.  
**Why it works:** Clutter is easier to spot and remove from a spacious start.

**Observable checks:**
- Are related items so far apart that they no longer read as a group?
- Are items so close that labels, tooltips or charts collide?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Interpretation (ours, not stated by the PDF):**
- The lesson is a process; the over-spaced state is a starting point, not a target.

**Related:** [WS-01](08-whitespace.md#ws-01)

<a id="ws-03"></a>
## WS-03 - Use a spacing and sizing scale; avoid arbitrary values

Choose a base unit and use only its multiples (e.g. 4 → 4, 8, 16, 24, 32px); odd values like 19px or 31px break rhythm.

- **Source:** PDF 28 (printed 27), 29 (printed 28)
- **Applies when:** All spacing, padding, gaps and component sizes.

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Establish a base unit and multiples, e.g. 4: 4, 8, 16, 24, 32px; multiples of 2, 4 or 6 are common.
- A standard scale gives a consistent look, faster adjustments and proportion, aligns with proximity (e.g. related items 8px apart) and reduces cognitive load.
- Avoid random numbers such as 31px or 19px: they disrupt rhythm, look disjointed and are hard to remember and reapply.

**Mistake:** Spacing values such as 7, 19, 21px chosen by eye, with no distinction between within-group and between-group gaps.  
**Effect:** Uneven rhythm and weak grouping.

**Correction:** Snap all spacing to the scale and use larger steps for larger separations (the source form uses 8 label→input, 24 between fields, 40 between sections).  
**Why it works:** A shared scale yields repeatable, proportional rhythm.

**Observable checks:**
- List all margin/padding/gap values: are they all multiples of the chosen base (e.g. 4)?
- Are there odd one-off values (e.g. 7px, 19px, 31px)?

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Interpretation (ours, not stated by the PDF):**
- The source's own shadow examples (DEP-04) use values like 19 and 56; the scale rule is stated for spacing and sizing.

**Source issues / ambiguity:**
- On this page the correct example is on the LEFT and the incorrect on the RIGHT, the reverse of most pages.

**Related:** [PRX-01](03-proximity.md#prx-01), [ALN-04](05-alignment.md#aln-04)

<a id="ws-04"></a>
## WS-04 - Don't stretch forms to fill wide screens

On large displays, give fields and buttons only the width they need inside a clearly defined box, with whitespace around it.

- **Source:** PDF 130 (printed 129), 131 (printed 130)
- **Applies when:** Sign-up, login and checkout forms on desktop widths (1440px and wider).

**What the PDF states** (paraphrased):
- Stretching a sign-up form or checkout flow to fill the screen is wrong: full-width inputs and CTAs overwhelm and look cluttered, and long lines of text or fields reduce comprehension.
- Concentrate fields in a clearly defined box with ample whitespace; whitespace is not wasted, it separates sections and draws attention. A different background colour or subtle image around it can enhance this.

**Mistake:** Inputs and Sign up button spanning almost the full page width.  
**Effect:** Overwhelming, cluttered, harder to read and complete.

**Correction:** Constrain the form to a centred card of modest width on a contrasting page background.  
**Why it works:** Focuses attention and keeps field widths proportional to content.

**Observable checks:**
- At 1440px, how wide are inputs and the primary button? Flag forms whose fields span most of the viewport.

**Exceptions / limits supported by the source:**
- None stated by the source.

**Interpretation (ours, not stated by the PDF):**
- The corrected card is roughly 450px wide in the figure; the source gives no number.

**Related:** [TYP-04](15-typography.md#typ-04), [FRM-02](17-forms.md#frm-02), [WS-01](08-whitespace.md#ws-01)
